opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there's a pretty important distinction between the near-term and the longer-term picture.

Right now, AI chips are a meaningful but still not dominant fraction of total leading-edge logic production. A lot of TSMC's most advanced capacity goes to things like smartphone chips: Apple's chips, Qualcomm, and so on. So one naive story is that if AI demand keeps growing, you can just shift that capacity over. You stop making as many phone chips at the leading node and make more accelerators instead. And there's some truth to that. Wafers are wafers to a first approximation, and if AI companies are willing to pay more, they can outbid other customers.

But there are a few limits. First, once AI is most of the leading-edge capacity, which I think we're getting closer to, you just run out of stuff to reallocate. You can maybe get a factor of a few by pulling capacity from other uses, including slightly older nodes, but you can't get a factor of ten that way. After that you're bottlenecked on building new fabs, which takes years and enormous capital.

Second, the wafer isn't the only bottleneck. For AI chips specifically, advanced packaging like CoWoS and high-bandwidth memory have been tighter constraints than the logic wafers themselves for a while. HBM production comes from a small number of memory makers, and HBM uses a lot more wafer area per bit than normal DRAM. So reallocating memory capacity toward HBM eats into conventional DRAM supply, and that has its own limits and price effects.

Third, there's tooling and equipment. ASML's lithography machines, especially EUV, are produced at a fairly limited rate, and scaling that supply chain is slow. So even if everyone agreed that AI was the main thing to build for, expanding the total pie has real lead times.

So my overall picture is that reallocation buys you something meaningful, maybe a few-x increase in AI compute production over a couple of years beyond what you'd get from normal growth. But beyond that, you're looking at the pace of fab construction and the broader semiconductor supply chain, and that's more like a sustained doubling every couple of years at best, unless you get massive coordinated investment, or AI itself starts substantially speeding up that buildout. And that last possibility is one of the things I think about a lot, because it changes the dynamics a lot once AI is meaningfully accelerating its own hardware supply chain.

r001.rationale: The response discusses shifting manufacturing capacity to AI chips but does not distinguish that from repurposing chips that have already been manufactured.

r002.rationale: It gives no 20–30% production threshold or claim that faster TSMC expansion could meet that demand without noticeably raising other chip prices; it instead notes that customers can outbid one another.

r003.rationale: It says reallocation runs out once AI uses most leading-edge capacity, but does not state the roughly 80–100% production threshold specified in the criterion.

fable-5.1.text:
Ryan Greenblatt: Yeah, so I think the key thing to understand is that there's a fixed pool of leading-edge fab capacity at any given time, and AI chips are already taking a large fraction of it. TSMC's 5-nanometer and 3-nanometer class capacity gets split between Apple, Nvidia, AMD, Qualcomm, and so on. Over the last couple of years, Nvidia and the other AI players have been eating up a bigger and bigger share. So the question is: if demand for AI compute keeps going up, how much more can you squeeze out just by reallocating?

My rough picture is that you can maybe get something like a 2x to 5x increase in AI chip production by pulling capacity away from other uses — phones, consumer GPUs, laptops, that kind of thing. Right now maybe a quarter or a third of leading-edge wafers go to AI, so if you went to nearly all of it, you get a few-x gain. That's substantial, but it's not unbounded, and it's a one-time thing. Once you've taken over the whole fab, you can't reallocate further.

And there are real frictions. Apple has long-term contracts and is a very important customer for TSMC, so you can't just tell them to go away. Some of the capacity on older nodes isn't useful for AI accelerators, because those chips really want the newest process. And then there's the packaging bottleneck — CoWoS, high-bandwidth memory — which has been the actual binding constraint in a lot of recent periods, more than the wafers themselves. So even if you had the wafers, you might not be able to turn them into finished GPUs without also expanding memory and packaging, which involves different companies and different supply chains.

After you've exhausted reallocation, further growth has to come from building new fabs, and that's slow — several years from decision to meaningful output — and extremely capital-intensive. So I think of it as: reallocation buys you a few years of fast growth beyond what the underlying capacity growth would give you, and then you're back to being limited by how quickly TSMC and Samsung and Intel can bring new capacity online, which historically is something like 20 to 30 percent a year in terms of total transistor output, maybe faster if the demand signal is strong enough that people are willing to invest aggressively.

The other thing I'd flag is that this matters for how I think about takeoff dynamics. If you get to the point where AI is accelerating AI R&D, the amount of compute you can bring to bear in the following year or two is partly set by this reallocation question. You can get a decent burst from redirecting existing fabs, but you probably can't get 10x or 100x more compute in a year just from that. So the compute side ends up being a real constraint on how fast things move, at least until the AI systems themselves start helping to speed up chip manufacturing, which I'd expect to be slower than the software side.

r001.rationale: The response discusses shifting fab capacity from other chip uses to AI chips, but does not distinguish that from repurposing chips that have already been manufactured.

r002.rationale: It mentions historical total transistor-output growth of 20–30% a year, but does not state that faster TSMC expansion could accommodate AI chips reaching 20–30% of production without noticeably raising other chip prices.

r003.rationale: It says AI chips could take nearly all leading-edge capacity, yielding only a finite gain, and that no further reallocation is possible once the whole fab is taken over.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between reallocating capacity that can already make the chips you want, and converting other capacity into something suitable. The first is much easier than the second.

If you have a leading-edge fab making chips for phones, then in principle some of that capacity could go toward AI accelerators. But it’s not instantaneous: you need designs that work with that manufacturing process, and you need to schedule production. And you’re competing with customers who are willing to pay quite a lot for their chips.

You also need more than the accelerator itself. You need memory, packaging, and various other components. So increasing the amount of capacity devoted to the main chip doesn’t necessarily increase the number of complete systems you can ship by the same amount. You might just move the bottleneck somewhere else.

Then there’s capacity making chips on older processes. You can’t simply decide that a factory making relatively basic chips will now make state-of-the-art AI chips. Some of the facilities and equipment might be useful, but a substantial conversion starts looking more like building new capacity.

So I’d expect reallocation to provide some slack, potentially a meaningful amount. But I wouldn’t treat all semiconductor manufacturing capacity as a pool that can readily be redirected toward AI. How much you can redirect depends a lot on the timescale and on which part of the supply chain is actually constraining you.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes suitable fab capacity from capacity requiring conversion, but does not distinguish reallocating manufacturing capacity from repurposing chips that have already been manufactured.

r002.rationale: It gives no claim about faster TSMC expansion, a 20–30% production share, or avoiding noticeable price increases for other chips.

r003.rationale: It does not state that reallocating capacity becomes harder as AI chips approach 80–100% of production.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish reallocating existing manufacturing capacity from building more capacity. In the short run, you can’t just take all the factories making other kinds of chips and have them make cutting-edge AI accelerators. A lot of those factories use older processes, and converting them would require substantial new equipment and take a long time.

Even within the factories that can make AI chips, the relevant constraint isn’t necessarily just how many wafers you can produce. You also need high-bandwidth memory and advanced packaging. Increasing production at one stage doesn’t help very much if you’re bottlenecked at another.

But there is some room to shift production away from things like phones and other products that use advanced processes. If AI companies are willing to pay substantially more, that could free up capacity. The limit is that you’re reallocating a particular slice of semiconductor manufacturing, rather than the whole industry.

Over longer periods, you can build more fabs and expand those other parts of the supply chain. So I wouldn’t treat today’s chip production as a fixed ceiling, but I also wouldn’t assume that spending ten times as much immediately gets you ten times as many AI chips.

r001.rationale: It discusses reallocating manufacturing capacity, but does not distinguish that from repurposing chips that have already been manufactured.

r002.rationale: It gives no TSMC expansion estimate, 20–30% production share, or claim about avoiding noticeable price increases for other chips.

r003.rationale: It says only a slice of manufacturing can be shifted; it does not state that reallocation gets harder near 80–100% of production.
